subject: Cognitive Science
title: The Framing Effect
description: A 60-second lesson on The Framing Effect.

hook.text: A surgery has a 90% survival rate. The same surgery has a 10% mortality rate. Which sounds better?

buildup.text: Same numbers, different frames. Yet people overwhelmingly prefer the 'survival' frame and reject 'mortality.'

discovery.text: The framing effect: how information is presented changes the decision, even when the facts are identical.

twist.text: Doctors are susceptible too. Framing a treatment as '200 saved out of 600' versus '400 die' shifts their recommendations.

climax.text: Politicians, advertisers, and negotiators all exploit framing. The fact is the same—the lens changes everything.

punchline.text: Same fact, different frame, different choice.

quiz.question: What does the framing effect demonstrate?
options: Presentation changes decisions even with identical facts

details.summary: How a choice is framed dramatically changes decisions. People prefer surgery with a 90 percent survival rate over surgery with a 10 percent mortality rate, even though they are identical. Framing effects reveal that decisions depend on presentation, not just objective information.
details.whyItMatters: Framing effects show that rational choice is a myth when presentation changes preferences. This has enormous implications for medicine, policy, marketing, and law.
takeaways: Identical options framed differently produce different choices
Positive frames promote risk aversion; negative frames promote risk seeking
Framing effects persist even when people are aware of them

faq.question: What is the classic framing experiment?
faq.answer: Tversky and Kahneman presented the Asian disease problem. When framed as saving 200 of 600 people, most chose the sure option. When framed as 400 will die, most chose the risky gamble. Same outcomes, different words, completely different preferences.

faq.question: Can people overcome framing effects?
faq.answer: Awareness reduces but does not eliminate framing effects. Converting information to a common format like percentages helps. Experienced decision-makers in a specific domain are less susceptible but not immune. Framing taps into automatic processing that deliberation cannot fully override.
